'''Robin Phillips''' [[Order of Canada|OC]] (28 February 1940 – 25 July 2015) was an English [[actor]] and [[film director]].

== Life ==
He was born in [[Haslemere]], [[Surrey]] in 1940<ref>{{cite news|last=Morrow|first=Martin|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/theatre-and-performance/canadian-stage-greats-have-actor-director-robin-phillips-to-thank/article25809583/|title=Canadian stage greats have actor, director Robin Phillips to thank|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=31 July 2015|quote=(not 1942, as most biographies indicate). According to Joe Mandel, Mr. Phillips’s long-time partner, the incorrect date was listed on his first British passport and remained on the records thereafter.}}</ref><ref name="nyt">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/03/theater/robin-phillips-director-who-revitalized-canadas-stratford-festival-dies-at-75.html?_r=0|last=Weber|first=Bruce|date=2 August 2015|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Robin Phillips, Director, Dies at 75; Revitalized Canada's Stratford Festival}}</ref> to Ellen Anne ([[married and maiden names|née]] Barfoot) and James William Phillips.<ref>[http://www.filmreference.com/film/40/Robin-Phillips.html Robin Phillips profile at FilmReference.com]</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-109899|title=Phillips, Robin (1940–2015), director, designer, and actor|website=oxforddnb.com|year=2019|language=en|doi=10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.013.109899|access-date=2019-10-11|last1=Jennings|first1=Alex|isbn=9780198614128}}</ref> He trained at the [[Bristol Old Vic]], where a contemporary was [[Patrick Stewart]], and worked as an actor and director for many years in the [[United Kingdom]], finishing as artistic director at the [[Greenwich Theatre]] from 1973 to 1975.

He was hired as artistic director at the [[Stratford Festival]] in Canada in 1975, where he spent six seasons directing many productions and cultivating new talent. [[Maggie Smith]], [[Richard Monette]], [[Martha Henry]] and [[Brian Bedford]], among others, were prominently featured during his tenure, and many of his Shakespearean, classical, and contemporary productions won widespread acclaim.<ref>[http://www.canadiantheatre.com/dict.pl?term=Robin%20Phillips Canadian Theatre Encyclopedia]</ref><ref>[[Maurice Good]]. "Every inch a Lear": a rehearsal journal of "King Lear" with [[Peter Ustinov]] and the Stratford Festival Company, directed by Robin Phillips. Sono Nis Press, 1982. {{ISBN|978-0-919203-26-6}}</ref><ref name=cbcda-rprs>{{cite web|title=Stratford Gold: Robin Phillips revitalizes Stratford|url=https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/1464491829|publisher=CBC Digital Archives|access-date=4 April 2019|year=2002}} Includes 24min video.</ref><ref>{{cite web | url =https://archives.stratfordfestival.ca/AIS/Details/people/8910 | title = Robin Phillips directing credits | website = Stratford Festival Archives | access-date = 2019-06-03}}</ref> In a review of Phillips' 1977 Stratford production of [[Richard III (play)|Richard III]] with Bedford in the title role, ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'' theatre critic [[John Fraser (journalist)|John Fraser]] wrote: "The production Phillips has mounted is stunning, crackling with nuances and details that are spellbinding, while radiating an over-all economy of dramatic management that demands an intense involvement from any audience".<ref name=fraser>{{Citation|last=Fraser|first=John|title=Richard III: dark byways of the soul|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=10 June 1977|page=16}}</ref> Veteran Stratford actor and director [[William Hutt (actor)|William Hutt]] compared Phillips to earlier artistic directors by saying: "With [[Tyrone Guthrie|Guthrie]], the heartbeat of a production was loud, obvious, robust and healthy. With [[Michael Langham|Langham]], rhythmic, predictable and safe. With [[Jean Gascon|Gascon]] it ran fast; you suspected high blood pressure. With Phillips the heartbeat is thunderingly silent: it’s the audience’s hearts you hear beating”.<ref name=cobb>{{Citation|last=Cobb|first=David|title=The master of Stratford|newspaper=Macleans|date=30 May 1977|page=34|url=https://archive.macleans.ca/article/1977/5/30/the-master-of-stratford|access-date=3 June 2019}}</ref>

Phillips' energy seemed boundless during his time at the Stratford helm. He directed 36 productions in six seasons (his predecessor [[Jean Gascon]] directed 17 productions in seven seasons), and the company, audience, and overall scale of the organization grew considerably.<ref name="cbcda-rprs"/><ref>{{cite AV media | date = 10 August 1997 | title = Dialogue: Robin Phillips | url = https://www.tvo.org/video/archive/robin-phillips | access-date = 11 June 2019 | publisher = TV Ontario }}</ref> But the workload took its toll: exhaustion was cited as the primary reason for his departure when he resigned during the 1980 season.<ref>Martin Knelman, ''A Stratford Tempest''. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1982, 240 p. {{ISBN|978-0-7710-4542-4}}</ref> He would later become artistic director at the [[Grand Theatre (London, Ontario)|Grand Theatre]] in [[London, Ontario]] and return to Stratford to direct the Young Company in 1987–88. He was also director general at the [[Citadel Theatre]] in [[Edmonton]] from 1990 to 1995.

He directed a musical version of ''[[Jekyll & Hyde (musical)|Jekyll & Hyde]]'' (1997) on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] (winning the [[Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Set Design]] for his contribution to the scenic design); ''[[Long Day's Journey into Night]]'' in London's [[West End theatre|West End]] in 2000; and a stage version of ''[[Larry's Party]]'' at [[Canadian Stage]] and the [[National Arts Centre]] in 2001.

Phillips was appointed an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]] in 2005.<ref name="gg">{{cite web |title=Order of Canada |website=The [[Governor General of Canada]]
|url=http://www.gg.ca/honour.aspx?id=10661&t=12 |access-date=13 March 2017}}</ref> The citation read, in part, "Robin Phillips is revered amongst members of Canada's acting community. ... A tremendous asset to the cultural life of Canada, he is also credited with bringing new life to the Citadel Theatre in Edmonton and to theatres across the country."<ref name="gg"/>
In 2010, Phillips received the [[Governor General's Performing Arts Award]] for Lifetime Artistic Achievement, Canada's highest honour in the performing arts.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robin Phillips biography|url=http://ggpaa.ca/award-recipients/2010/phillips-robin.aspx|publisher=Governor General's Performing Arts Awards Foundation|access-date=11 February 2015}}</ref>

Phillips died in his sleep on 25 July 2015, after a prolonged illness.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/arts/robin-phillips-former-head-of-stratford-festival-dead-at-73-1.3168217 | title=Robin Phillips, former head of Stratford Festival, dead at 73 | publisher=CBC News | date=26 July 2015 | access-date=26 July 2015 }}</ref><ref name="nyt" /> He was survived by a younger sister, Hilary, and by his partner, Joe Mandel (1936–2023), whom he first met in 1962 but who became his partner in 1971.<ref name=Obit>Obituary for Robin Phillips in ''[[The Guardian]]'' - 30 July 2015</ref>

==In film==

Though none of his stage productions were captured on film, Phillips is featured in the documentary ''Robin and Mark and Richard III'', in which he guides veteran TV actor [[Mark McKinney]] through some key scenes in [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare's]] [[Richard III (play)|Richard III]]. Its creators [[Susan Coyne]] and [[Martha Burns]] had both been directed and mentored by Phillips earlier in their careers, and wanted to capture some of his technique coaching McKinney, a Shakespeare novice. The film was released in 2016, shortly after Phillips' death.<ref>{{cite web|title=Review: ROBIN AND MARK AND RICHARD III|url=http://slotkinletter.com/2016/04/review-robin-and-mark-and-richard-iii|access-date=15 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Doc screening features Canadian theatre & TV legends|url=https://finearts.uvic.ca/research/blog/2017/09/12/doc-screening-features-canadian-theatre-tv-legends|access-date=15 April 2018}}</ref>
